title: I’m building a system that turns your phone + PC into one intelligent gaming setup (SecondScreen OS)
author: Capable_Yam3580
selftext:
Hey everyone,

I’ve been working on an idea and wanted to share it here to get feedback from gamers, devs, and anyone interested in gaming tech.



# 🧠 The idea

Instead of using your phone as just a controller or using screen mirroring apps, I’m building something different:

👉 A system where your phone becomes a **live second brain for your PC games**

Not just buttons. Not just remote control.

But a **dynamic, intelligent layer that understands what’s happening in the game in real time.**



# 🎮 What it does

When you connect your PC and phone on the same WiFi:

# 🖥️ PC side:

* Runs a lightweight agent
* Sends real-time game state / events

# 📱 Phone side:

* Shows a **dynamic UI that changes per game**
* Displays live info (HP, ammo, cooldowns, map, inventory)
* Gives quick actions based on what’s happening
* Can act like an adaptive controller OR assistant



# 🔥 Example

In an FPS game:

* Phone shows ammo, grenades, enemy alerts
* Quick “reload / switch weapon / heal” buttons
* Optional AI suggestions like “low ammo, reload now”

In racing games:

* Steering controls
* Track overview
* Pit stop / boost timing

In RPGs:

* Inventory shortcuts
* Ability cooldown tracker
* Quest tracking panel



# 🚨 What makes it different

Most tools today are either:

* Screen mirroring (Steam Link, Remote Play)
* Or static gamepads (Monect, controller apps)

This is different because:

👉 The phone UI is **alive and context-aware**  
👉 It changes depending on what is happening in-game  
👉 It acts like a **second intelligence layer**, not just input device



# 🧩 Vision

The goal is to create a “dual-screen gaming OS layer” where:

* PC = execution (game runs here)
* Phone = intelligence + control + awareness

Basically:  
👉 one game, two coordinated devices



# 💬 Honest question

Would you actually use something like this?

And what would be the most useful feature for you:

* better controls?
* live stats?
* AI assistance?
* or something else?

I’m still shaping the idea, so feedback is really appreciated.

comments.author: Aromatic-Low-4578
comments.body:
This doesn't sound particularly new, mostly just treating it like a second monitor.  

I could see it being super impactful though if for example taking or making phone calls was part of the gameplay, then it could be super immersive to use a real phone as a controller.  Getting 'texts' from a character in the game could be really interesting too.

replies.author: Capable_Yam3580
replies.body:
You’re basically right that “phone as second monitor/controller” on its own isn’t new — a lot of companion apps and remote play ideas have already tried that.

Where it *does* get interesting is when the phone stops being just a display/input and becomes part of the game’s *systems*. Like you said: calls, texts, notifications, even timing-based interruptions. That turns it into an “in-world device” instead of an external tool.

The key difference is immersion vs utility:

* Second screen → convenience layer
* Integrated phone mechanics → gameplay layer

If a game actually uses real-world behaviors (incoming calls you have to answer, messages that arrive while you’re playing, decisions made through real-time communication), then it starts to feel less like a controller and more like the game leaking into your actual environment — that’s where it becomes impactful.

The hard part is balancing that without making it annoying or intrusive, especially for players who don’t want their real phone constantly hijacked.

So yeah — the base idea is old, but the “phone as narrative + mechanic engine” angle is where it becomes something genuinely new.     
what do you think?

replies.author: Capable_Yam3580
replies.body:
That was basically the main idea — real-time interaction between the game world and the real-world environment, not just a second screen or companion app.

The goal is to go beyond traditional input/output and create a layer where the game actively communicates with the player in real time through different channels (calls, messages, environmental triggers), making the experience feel more like a living system than a static screen.

Another direction that could make it feel truly new is expanding it into a shared local experience layer — similar to how 7D cinema adds environmental effects, but in a digital way. For example, devices connected to the same WiFi (phones, speakers, smart lights, maybe even other screens) could synchronize and react to in-game events together. So the environment itself becomes part of the game feedback loop.

In that sense, it’s not just about immersion on a single device, but about turning the surrounding connected space into an interactive extension of the game world.
